n: Ephraim chases the wind—the scorching east wind that brings only ruin. It multiplies lies and violence, making treaties with Assyria while sending olive oil as gifts to Egypt. Playing both sides was empty and dangerous.

f.g: Olive oil sent as tribute or bribe to secure an alliance.

n: God also has a case against Judah, and will repay “Jacob”—all Israel—for its ways.
Hosea recalls their ancestor Jacob, who grabbed his brother’s heel in the womb and, as a man, struggled with God. Like their father, the nation has been a grasping schemer.

f.w: He took his brother by the heel in the womb

n: Jacob wrestled with the angel and prevailed—but notice how: he wept and begged for a blessing. At Bethel God met him and spoke with “us”—his descendants too. Jacob’s true strength was in humble pleading.

f.w: he wept, and made supplication unto him

n: This God is the LORD, the God of hosts; “the LORD” (Jehovah) is the name by which He is to be remembered. Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah to be the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.g: His name of remembrance is YHWH (Jehovah).

n: Like Jacob, Israel must return to God, practice loyal love and justice, and wait on Him continually. This is Hosea’s message in a nutshell.
Israel has become like a dishonest trader with rigged scales who loves to cheat. The Hebrew word for merchant is “Canaanite”—Israel has become like the people they displaced.
Ephraim boasts: “I’m rich! I earned it all myself, and no one can find any wrongdoing in me.” Wealth has blinded them to their sin.

The Lord, who has been Israel’s God since Egypt, will make them live in tents again—as in the wilderness or at the Feast of Tabernacles. It is both a judgment (losing their homes) and a hope (a fresh start with God).

f.w: make thee to dwell in tabernacles

n: God spoke through the prophets, gave many visions, and taught through parables and symbols. Israel had no lack of guidance.

f.w: I have also spoken by the prophets

n: Gilead is full of wickedness and emptiness; Gilgal’s sacrifices of bulls are worthless. Their altars will become piles of stones in plowed fields—a pun on Gilgal and the Hebrew word for stone heaps (gallim).
Jacob fled to Aram (Syria) and served as a shepherd to earn his wives. Hosea reminds them of their humble origins.

f.w: Jacob fled into the country of Syria

n: By a prophet—Moses—the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt and cared for them. In contrast to Jacob’s labor for a wife, God worked through prophets to save His people. Israel should listen to prophets now too.

f.w: by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt

n: Ephraim has bitterly provoked God. Their bloodguilt will remain on them, and the Lord will repay their contempt.

f.w: shall he leave his blood upon him
f.g: He will hold them responsible for their bloodshed.
